html:
The Palouse, or Palus, are a Sahaptin speaking people of the Columbia Plateau, from the Palouse River and the lower Snake River in southeastern Washington. The rolling Palouse hills, now wheat country, are named after them, and so is the Appaloosa horse, bred on this land.

They fished salmon, dug camas and other roots and, after horses came in the 1700s, became skilled horse breeders. They were close to the Nez Perce, Cayuse and Yakama, and also had ties with the Spokane. The Palouse did not sign the 1855 treaties and mostly refused reservations. Some fought with the Nez Perce in the Nez Perce War of 1877. Their descendants live today on the Colville, Yakama, Nez Perce and Umatilla reservations.
